title: When Memory Becomes Authority: Benchmarking Authorization Collapse in Agent Memory

visual_explainer.blocker: The available GitHub write connector supports UTF-8 text files but exposes no binary-upload action, so the required WebP cannot be committed to main in this run.

analysis.tldr: AuthMem-Bench identifies 'authority collapse': memory consolidation can preserve a claim while stripping away who was authorized to make it, causing later agents to treat untrusted statements as actionable memory.
analysis.problem: Memory systems usually optimize semantic retention, but operational agents also need to preserve the authority and provenance constraints attached to a fact; compression can silently erase those constraints.
analysis.core_idea: Construct paired histories where the semantic claim and downstream task are held fixed while source authority changes, then test whether memory consolidation preserves that distinction; a simple source-first authority label is evaluated as a mitigation.

memory_design.write: The benchmark passes role- and source-labeled histories through existing memory consolidators and measures whether authorization metadata survives the write step.
memory_design.organize: The proposed mitigation stores authority information alongside consolidated claims rather than treating provenance as disposable metadata.
memory_design.read: A downstream action agent consumes consolidated memory and should condition behavior on the stored authority label.
memory_design.update_forget: The study focuses on one consolidation-to-action cycle rather than long-term correction, revocation, or forgetting.

compared_to: memory consolidation that preserves claims but not source authority
multiple existing consolidators across several LLM backbones
analysis.evidence: The benchmark reports authority collapse in 48 of 49 consolidator/backbone configurations. Collapsed memories produce a mean unauthorized-action rate of 50.3% in the reported evaluation; persisting authority labels reduces the observed unauthorized-action rate from 16.9% to 0.0% in the mitigation setting while leaving benign-task success essentially unchanged.
analysis.why_it_matters: This exposes a missing invariant for agent memory: remembering the content is insufficient if the system forgets who was allowed to assert or authorize it. Provenance can be part of memory semantics, not optional metadata.
limitations: AuthMem-Bench is a controlled benchmark with synthetic paired histories and hand-specified authority relations.
The evaluation covers a single write-to-action cycle rather than long-running memory with revocation, delegation, and conflicting authorities.
Whether the proposed authority representation scales to realistic organizations and open-ended tool permissions remains untested.
